analysis.one_liner: Repeals the mandated transfer of the sacred Oak Flat site to a copper mining company.
analysis.headline: The bill to cancel the Oak Flat land handoff never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the 114th Congress ended, despite 44 cosponsors including 3 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2014 defense bill quietly ordered the federal government to hand 2,422 acres of the Tonto National Forest — Oak Flat, a sacred site for the San Carlos Apache Tribe and other tribes — to Resolution Copper, a mining company. The Save Oak Flat Act would cancel that transfer, keeping the land public and protected. Instead of getting a vote, the bill was sent to a House committee and its subcommittees and sat there until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribes that worship at Oak Flat, and everyone who uses or values public land and Southeast Arizona's water supply. The bill would also preserve standard environmental review, which the 2014 transfer bypassed.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of the 2014 defense bill that mandates transferring 2,422 acres of Forest Service land at Oak Flat to Resolution Copper, keeping the land public.
Stops a mining method the bill text says will make the surface subside and collapse, permanently destroying a tribal place of worship.
Avoids depleting and contaminating water the bill text says would seep into drinking water supplies.
Restores ordinary environmental review and tribal consultation, which the 2014 provision required the government to bypass regardless of its findings.

analysis.who_pays: Resolution Copper and its parent companies, which lose the federally mandated swap of 2,422 acres for one of the largest undeveloped copper deposits in North America. Arizona communities hoping for mine jobs would also give that up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Resolution Copper and its parent companies

drawbacks.text: The land exchange was designed to swap protected acreage for private parcels, and repealing it cancels a negotiated deal that included conservation parcels and consultation steps, not just the handover itself.

The copper deposit beneath Oak Flat is a major domestic supply of a metal used in wiring, electrification, and defense; blocking the mine forfeits those jobs and production, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill asks a company to give up a congressionally mandated land swap that was attached to a defense bill without ever getting a standalone vote in either chamber. Against that is the permanent loss of a sacred site, likely collapse of the surface, and risks to a desert aquifer — costs that would fall on tribes and local communities with no remedy afterward. Weighing those, the protection side carries the heavier cost of failure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to three of its subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Introduced June 17, 2015, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources; it never advanced past committee.
On July 1, 2015, it was referred to three subcommittees — Energy and Mineral Resources, Federal Lands, and Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs — and no action followed.
The bill attracted 44 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans, but no markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 114th Congress expired.
The bill's own findings state the underlying land transfer was attached to the 2015 defense bill without majority support in either chamber and without an allowed vote on removing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Resolution Copper and its parent companies are better off: the mandated land exchange remained on the books, uncontested by any vote, and the mining project could keep moving through its federal review. Tribes and public-land users got nothing for two more years.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Resolution Copper and its parent mining firms

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Save Oak Flat Act to repeal the Oak Flat land transfer.

for.name: San Carlos Apache Tribe and allied tribes
for.role: Tribal nations for whom Oak Flat is a sacred site
for.what_they_did: Opposed the land transfer and supported repeal, as described in the bill's findings.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee majority that controlled the calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in subcommittee referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Resolution Copper
against.role: Mining company (owned by Rio Tinto and BHP) set to receive Oak Flat
against.what_they_did: Stood to gain the mandated land transfer and had pursued the exchange for years; its project continued under the 2014 law while repeal stalled.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 41 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but the bill died in a committee run by the House Republican majority without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper, owned by Rio Tinto and BHP)
industries.note: The company keeps a congressionally mandated transfer of 2,422 acres of public forest land — including a tribal sacred site — that the bill would have repealed. The transfer requires the government to convey the land regardless of what environmental review finds.

industries.industry: Copper-dependent manufacturers and defense supply chains
industries.note: Repealing the land exchange keeps a major copper deposit off the production schedule, forgoing domestic supply of a metal used in wiring, electrification, and defense. This is the strongest good-faith cost of the bill.
